API reference¶

Data loading¶

Load the NASA/UCI Airfoil Self-Noise dataset.

The dataset contains 1503 aerodynamic/acoustic measurements of NACA 0012 airfoils taken in a wind tunnel. Five input features describe the test conditions and one target, the scaled sound pressure level, describes the measured noise.

The Excel file is expected at data/airfoil_self_noise.xlsx, where it is committed to the repository (it is small, about 75 kB), so a fresh clone can run every script.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> df = load_airfoil_data()
>>> df.columns.tolist()[-1]
'spl_db'

Input checks and prediction¶

Checks that refuse missing, invalid or out-of-range inputs before predicting.

A prediction is only trustworthy for inputs like the ones the model was trained on. Instead of guessing, the checks below stop with an error that names the offending column(s), row(s) and value(s). Nothing is ever filled in (imputed) or silently clipped: a wrong guess would give a confident-looking but meaningless noise prediction.

The checks run in this order (validate_inputs()):

  1. Missing (MissingInputError): a required column is absent, or a value is empty/NaN.

  2. Invalid (InvalidInputError): a value is not a number, or is physically impossible:

    • frequency, chord, velocity and displacement thickness must be greater than 0. Zero or negative values are impossible, and they would also break the physics-derived features: log10(f) needs f > 0, the Strouhal number f δ*/U divides by the velocity, and the Reynolds number U c / ν needs a positive velocity and chord;

    • the angle of attack must be 0 or more. The NACA 0012 is symmetric, so a negative angle is in principle the same flow mirrored. It could be treated as merely out of range, but the dataset gives only the suction-side displacement thickness, so a negative angle (which swaps the suction and pressure sides) cannot be described correctly by these inputs. It is therefore treated as invalid.

  3. Out of range (OutOfRangeError): a valid value outside the range the final model was trained on (FEATURE_RANGES, both the minimum and the maximum). Predicting there would be extrapolating to a new setup whose noise could follow different physics, for example a smaller chord with stronger tonal noise, or a higher speed. The shift tests showed the error grows sharply outside the training range.

What these checks do not catch. Each input is checked on its own. A combination of individually valid values that was never tested together (for example the largest chord at the highest angle) passes, even though it is also an extrapolation. See the “Valid inputs” section of the usage docs.

Example

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from functions.input_checks import validate_inputs
>>> validate_inputs(pd.DataFrame({"frequency_hz": [1000], "attack_angle_deg": [-2.0],
...     "chord_length_m": [0.1], "velocity_mps": [50.0],
...     "disp_thickness_m": [0.002]}))   
InvalidInputError: Invalid input: 'attack_angle_deg' must be >= 0 ...

Predict SPL for new inputs with the final model, refusing bad inputs.

This is the safe way to use the trained model on new conditions: predict_spl() first runs functions.input_checks.validate_inputs() (missing, invalid and out-of-range inputs stop with an error), then adds the physics features and predicts with the saved final MLP.

Physics features¶

Physics-derived features for the airfoil self-noise dataset.

The raw inputs are dimensional, but airfoil noise is governed largely by dimensionless groups. This module adds three engineered features computed row-wise from the raw columns, so they are recomputed on every load rather than stored in the Excel file.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.physics_features import add_physics_features
>>> df = add_physics_features(load_airfoil_data())
>>> df[["log_frequency", "strouhal", "reynolds"]].shape[1]
3
functions.physics_features.KINEMATIC_VISCOSITY_M2PS = 1.5e-05¶

Kinematic viscosity of air at roughly 20 °C (m^2/s), used for the Reynolds number. The wind-tunnel temperature is not recorded in the dataset, so a standard room-temperature value is assumed.

functions.physics_features.PHYSICS_FEATURES = ['log_frequency', 'strouhal', 'reynolds']¶

Names of the columns added by add_physics_features().

functions.physics_features.add_physics_features(df: pandas.DataFrame) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Return a copy of the dataset with physics-derived feature columns.

Adds:

  • log_frequency: log10(frequency_hz). Frequencies span about two decades, and acoustic spectra are naturally read on a log axis.

  • strouhal: frequency_hz * disp_thickness_m / velocity_mps. Uses the suction-side displacement thickness as the length scale, the scaling used for turbulent boundary-layer trailing-edge noise in the Brooks-Pope-Marcolini (BPM) model.

  • reynolds: velocity_mps * chord_length_m / nu, the chord-based Reynolds number with nu = KINEMATIC_VISCOSITY_M2PS.

Each feature depends only on its own row, so adding them before the train/validation/test split does not leak information between sets.

Parameters:

df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

Returns:

A new DataFrame with the original columns plus the columns listed in PHYSICS_FEATURES. The input DataFrame is not modified.

Data split¶

Grouped, chord-stratified test hold-out and 5-fold cross-validation split.

Each wind-tunnel setup (a unique chord length, free-stream velocity and angle of attack) contributes one noise spectrum of 8-19 rows. Rows from the same spectrum are strongly correlated, so whole setups are assigned to a split: a setup’s rows are never divided between training and validation/test.

The split is stratified on chord length because chord is the only variable tested at the same values throughout the dataset; the angles tested differ for every chord and some velocity/angle combinations were never measured.

Splitting happens on a table with one row per setup, so ordinary stratified splitters give a grouped split automatically. The result is mapped back onto the measurement rows as two columns:

  • setup_id: integer id of the setup, numbered in order of (chord, velocity, angle).

  • fold: 0 to N_FOLDS - 1 for cross-validation rows, or TEST_FOLD for rows in the held-out test set.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.make_folds import assign_folds, CV_SEEDS, TEST_FOLD
>>> raw = load_airfoil_data()
>>> for seed in CV_SEEDS:
...     df = assign_folds(raw, cv_seed=seed)
...     test = df[df["fold"] == TEST_FOLD]  # same setups for every seed
...     cv = df[df["fold"] != TEST_FOLD]

functions.make_folds.STRATIFY_ON = 'chord_length_m'¶

functions.make_folds.TEST_FRACTION = 0.15¶

functions.make_folds.TEST_FOLD = -1¶

fold value given to rows in the held-out test set.

functions.make_folds.TEST_SEED = 41¶

functions.make_folds.assign_folds(df: pandas.DataFrame, n_folds: int = 5, test_fraction: float = 0.15, cv_seed: int = 42, test_seed: int = 41) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Return a copy of the dataset with setup_id and fold columns.

First holds out test_fraction of the setups as a test set, then splits the remaining setups into n_folds cross-validation folds. Both steps are stratified on chord length and work on whole setups. For repeated CV, call once per seed in CV_SEEDS; the test set depends only on test_seed and so is identical across repeats.

Parameters:

  • df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data() (physics feature columns, if present, are carried through unchanged).

  • n_folds – Number of cross-validation folds.

  • test_fraction – Fraction of setups held out as the test set.

  • cv_seed – Random seed for shuffling setups into CV folds.

  • test_seed – Random seed for choosing the test hold-out.

Returns:

A new DataFrame with the original columns plus setup_id and fold. The input DataFrame is not modified.

Feature sets¶

Named input feature sets, so models can be compared on different inputs.

Each feature set is a list of column names. Any model in functions.models can be trained on any feature set, so swapping inputs is a matter of changing one name.

  • A: the five raw wind-tunnel inputs.

  • B: A plus the physics-derived features log_frequency, strouhal and reynolds. These columns only exist after functions.physics_features.add_physics_features() has been applied.

Example

>>> from functions.feature_sets import get_feature_columns
>>> get_feature_columns("B")[-3:]
['log_frequency', 'strouhal', 'reynolds']
functions.feature_sets.FEATURE_SETS = {'A': ['frequency_hz', 'attack_angle_deg', 'chord_length_m', 'velocity_mps', 'disp_thickness_m'], 'B': ['frequency_hz', 'attack_angle_deg', 'chord_length_m', 'velocity_mps', 'disp_thickness_m', 'log_frequency', 'strouhal', 'reynolds']}¶

Models¶

Model registry: every model is built as the same scikit-learn pipeline.

Each model returned by build_model() has the structure:

TransformedTargetRegressor(
    regressor=Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()),   # if scale_inputs
                        ("regressor", <estimator>)]),
    transformer=StandardScaler(),                       # scales spl_db
)

Because the scalers sit inside the estimator, calling fit on the training rows fits them on those rows only; validation and test rows are transformed with the training mean and standard deviation and never influence them.

Scaling the target to zero mean and unit variance matters for SVR (its epsilon tube and C are in target units) and for neural networks (output scale and loss magnitude). For the linear baseline neither scaling step changes the predictions, but it is applied anyway so every model runs through the same pipeline and the linear coefficients are comparable in size.

Registered models:

  • "linear": ordinary least squares, the baseline.

  • "mlp": a multi-layer perceptron (MLPRegressor) with early stopping. The layer sizes and alpha set here are only defaults; the values actually reported come from nested cross-validation in functions.tuning.

  • "mlp_final": the MLP with the frozen final settings FINAL_MLP, chosen from the nested-CV results, for use on FINAL_FEATURE_SET.

  • "mlp_runner_up": the cheaper alternative RUNNER_UP_MLP.

Later scripts (profiling, shift tests, the final hold-out run) must use FINAL_MODEL_NAME, FINAL_FEATURE_SET and these constants rather than retyping the values.

Tree-based models and SVR are planned; each is added as one ModelSpec entry in MODELS (trees do not need input scaling, so they would use scale_inputs=False).

Example

>>> from functions.models import build_model
>>> model = build_model("linear")
>>> model.fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_val)
functions.models.MLP_DEFAULTS = {'alpha': 0.001, 'early_stopping': True, 'hidden_layer_sizes': (64, 64), 'max_iter': 2000, 'n_iter_no_change': 20, 'random_state': 0, 'tol': 0.0001, 'validation_fraction': 0.1}¶

Type:

functions.models.FINAL_MLP = {'alpha': 1.0, 'hidden_layer_sizes': (128, 128)}¶

This setting won 7 of the 15 outer folds, more than any other, and had the lowest mean inner-CV RMSE of all 35 settings (2.50 dB). functions.models.coefficient_effects(model: TransformedTargetRegressor, feature_names: list[str]) → pd.Series | None[source]¶

Return a fitted linear model’s coefficients as dB per standard deviation.

Inside the pipeline both inputs and target are standardised, so each fitted coefficient is the change in SPL, in target standard deviations, for a one-standard-deviation change in that input with all other inputs held fixed. Multiplying by the target’s standard deviation turns this into dB per input standard deviation, which can be compared directly across features with very different units (Hz, m, m/s, Reynolds number).

Correlated inputs (e.g. frequency_hz and log_frequency in set B) share their effect between them, so individual coefficients can be large, of opposite sign and unstable between folds even when predictions are good. Look at the spread over folds before interpreting one.

Parameters:

  • model – A model from build_model() that has been fitted.

  • feature_names – Input columns in the order the model was fitted on.

Returns:

A Series indexed by feature name, in dB per input standard deviation, or None if the model has no linear coefficients or does not scale its inputs (raw-unit coefficients are not comparable across features).

Cross-validation and metrics¶

Repeated cross-validation, metrics and error breakdowns for any model.

cross_validate() trains a model from functions.models on a feature set from functions.feature_sets using the grouped folds from functions.make_folds, repeated for every seed in CV_SEEDS. It returns:

  • per-fold scores (RMSE, MAE, R², fit and predict time), and

  • out-of-fold (OOF) predictions: every cross-validation row predicted once per seed by the model that did not see it during training.

Rows in the held-out test set are dropped before anything is fitted, so this module never trains on, tunes on or scores the test set.

RMSE is the main metric. oof_rmse_breakdown() splits the OOF RMSE by chord length, free-stream velocity, angle-of-attack band and frequency band to show where a model’s errors come from. For linear models, coefficient_summary() reports each input’s effect in dB per standard deviation and how stable it is across folds.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.physics_features import add_physics_features
>>> from functions.evaluate import cross_validate, summarise, oof_rmse_breakdown
>>> data = add_physics_features(load_airfoil_data())
>>> result = cross_validate(data, "linear", "A")
>>> summarise(result)            
>>> oof_rmse_breakdown(result)

functions.evaluate.cross_validate(data: pandas.DataFrame, model_name: str, feature_set: str, cv_seeds: list[int] = [42, 43, 44]) → CVResult[source]¶

Run repeated grouped k-fold cross-validation for one model/feature set.

For each seed, functions.make_folds.assign_folds() assigns folds, the test hold-out is dropped, and for each fold a fresh model is fitted on the other folds and predicts the held-out fold. Fit and predict are timed separately with time.perf_counter().

Parameters:

  • model_name – Key of functions.models.MODELS.

  • feature_set – Key of functions.feature_sets.FEATURE_SETS.

  • cv_seeds – Seeds for repeated CV. Defaults to functions.make_folds.CV_SEEDS and should not be changed when comparing models.

Returns:

A CVResult with per-fold scores, OOF predictions and, for linear models, per-fold coefficients.

Raises:

KeyError – If the model or feature set name is unknown, or data is missing a column the feature set needs.

functions.evaluate.summarise(result: CVResult) → dict[str, float][source]¶

Summarise a CV run as one row of headline numbers.

Each metric is the mean and sample standard deviation of the per-fold validation scores over all folds of all seeds (15 for 5 folds x 3 seeds). Each fold scores a model on a batch of setups it never saw, so the standard deviation answers “how much does the score change from one batch of unseen setups to the next?”. This is wider than the spread of seed-level averages, which would only show how much the random fold shuffle matters. Timings are also averaged over all folds.

The mean of per-fold RMSEs is slightly different from the RMSE of all pooled OOF predictions, because the square root is taken per fold.

Parameters:

result – Output of cross_validate().

Returns:

A dict with model, feature_set, n_folds (number of fold scores averaged), rmse, rmse_std, mae, mae_std, r2, r2_std, fit_time_s and predict_time_s (mean seconds per fold).

functions.evaluate.oof_rmse_breakdown(result: CVResult) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Break the OOF RMSE down by chord, velocity, angle band and frequency band.

For each breakdown column and each group within it, RMSE is computed on that group’s OOF predictions separately for every seed, then averaged over seeds.

Parameters:

result – Output of cross_validate().

Returns:

A DataFrame with columns breakdown (which column was grouped on), group (the value or band label), n (rows per seed), rmse (mean over seeds, dB) and rmse_std (std over seeds).

functions.evaluate.coefficient_summary(result: CVResult) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Summarise a linear model’s per-fold coefficients.

Every (seed, fold) fit gives one coefficient per feature; this reports their mean and spread. A coefficient whose sign flips between folds, or whose std is comparable to its mean, is not reliably estimated and should not be given a physical interpretation.

Parameters:

result – Output of cross_validate().

Returns:

A DataFrame indexed by feature (in feature-set order) with columns effect_db_per_sd (mean over fits), std, min, max and sign_agreement (fraction of fits whose sign matches the mean’s). Empty if the model has no linear coefficients.

functions.evaluate.SETUP_COLUMNS = ['setup_id', 'chord_length_m', 'velocity_mps', 'attack_angle_deg']¶

Columns describing one wind-tunnel setup in per_setup_rmse().

functions.evaluate.per_setup_rmse(result: CVResult, data: pandas.DataFrame) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Out-of-fold error for every wind-tunnel setup (one noise spectrum each).

In each CV repeat a setup sits in exactly one validation fold, so it is predicted once per seed by a model that never saw it. The setup’s RMSE is computed separately for each seed and then averaged over seeds. The bias (mean of measured minus predicted) shows whether the model sits mostly above or below the measured spectrum.

Parameters:

  • result – Output of cross_validate() (or the tuned-MLP equivalent from functions.tuning).

  • data – The dataset the result was computed on.

Returns:

One row per setup, worst first, with columns setup_id, chord_length_m, velocity_mps, attack_angle_deg, n_rows (measurements in the spectrum), rmse (dB, mean over seeds), rmse_sd_seeds and bias (dB; positive means the model under-predicts).

Entry point that cross-validates models on feature sets and reports results.

Every combination of the requested models and feature sets is evaluated with repeated grouped 5-fold CV (functions.evaluate.cross_validate()). The test hold-out is never used. Defaults run the linear baseline on sets A and B:

python src/run_cv.py
python src/run_cv.py --models linear --feature-sets A

Results are printed and written as CSV files to results/:

  • cv_summary.csv: one row per model/feature set (validation RMSE, MAE, R² as mean and std over all 15 folds, 5 folds x 3 seeds; mean fit and predict time per fold).

  • cv_fold_scores.csv: scores and timings for every seed and fold.

  • cv_rmse_breakdown.csv: OOF RMSE by chord, velocity, angle band and frequency band.

  • cv_coefficients.csv: for linear models, each input’s effect in dB per standard deviation (mean and spread over all folds and seeds).

Rounded copies of the summary, breakdown and coefficient tables, and the results figures (functions.plot_results), are also written to doc/generated/ for the HTML results page; rebuild the docs afterwards to publish them.

Results figures¶

Figures of cross-validation results for the HTML results page.

Every function takes one or more functions.evaluate.CVResult objects and returns a matplotlib figure; save_result_figures() draws them all and writes PNGs. Each result keeps the same colour in every figure (first result blue, second orange, …), so a model/feature set is recognisable across the page. Measured data are drawn in neutral ink, never a series colour.

Figures that show individual predictions use one CV seed (functions.make_folds.CV_SEEDS [0] by default) so that every row appears exactly once.

Example

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from functions.evaluate import cross_validate
>>> from functions.plot_results import save_result_figures
>>> results = [cross_validate(data, "linear", fs) for fs in ("A", "B")]
>>> save_result_figures(data, results, Path("doc/generated"))

MLP tuning (nested cross-validation)¶

Nested cross-validation to tune and fairly score the MLP.

Why nested CV?

If the same folds were used both to pick the best hyperparameters and to report the score, the score would be optimistic: the chosen setting is partly the one that got lucky on those folds. Nested CV keeps the two jobs apart. An inner CV, run on the outer training rows only, picks the hyperparameters; the outer validation fold, which the inner CV never sees, then scores the chosen model. The outer scores are therefore honest estimates for unseen setups.

Procedure (nested_cv()), for each seed in CV_SEEDS and each outer fold:

  1. Drop the test hold-out (it is never used for training, tuning, early stopping or scoring here). Outer validation = rows of this fold; outer training = the other cross-validation rows.

  2. On the outer training rows only, GridSearchCV tries every setting in PARAM_GRID with an inner grouped 5-fold split (inner_splitter()). setup_id is passed as groups, so no setup is ever split between inner training and inner validation.

  3. The best setting is refitted on all outer training rows and scored on the outer validation fold (RMSE, MAE, R² in dB).

Known limitations (quotable in the report):

  • Early stopping uses random rows, not whole setups. MLPRegressor’s built-in early stopping holds back a random 10% of the rows it is given to decide when to stop. Rows from one setup are strongly correlated, so the held-back rows usually have near-identical neighbours from the same setup in the training part. The internal stopping check is therefore mildly optimistic, and training may stop a little later than ideal. This does not leak into the reported scores: the inner and outer validation folds are grouped by setup, and the early-stopping rows are taken only from the data being fitted, never from the fold being scored. MLPRegressor was deliberately not rewritten to fix this.

  • Inner folds are grouped but not stratified on chord. GroupKFold keeps setups together but does not balance chord lengths across inner folds (the outer folds are chord-stratified by functions.make_folds.assign_folds()).

  • Convergence. Fits that stop at max_iter rather than by early stopping are counted (_hit_max_iter()), not hidden. Warnings raised in parallel worker processes cannot be caught in the main process, so the count is collected as an extra “score” instead.

Example

>>> from functions.tuning import nested_cv
>>> result = nested_cv(data, "A", seeds=[42])   
>>> result.outer_scores[["seed", "fold", "rmse"]]

functions.tuning.refit_outer_predictions(data: pandas.DataFrame, outer_scores: pandas.DataFrame, feature_set: str, extra_params: dict | None = None, atol: float = 1e-06) → CVResult[source]¶

Rebuild the tuned MLP’s out-of-fold predictions from saved results.

tuning_outer_scores.csv records which setting won each outer fold but not the row-by-row predictions. Because the MLP has a fixed random_state and is trained on exactly the same rows, refitting the winning setting reproduces each fold’s model, and so its predictions, exactly. This takes seconds instead of re-running the whole nested CV. Each refitted fold’s RMSE is checked against the saved value as proof.

Parameters:

  • data – Dataset with every column the feature set needs.

  • outer_scores – The saved TuningResult.outer_scores table (e.g. read from results/tuning_outer_scores.csv).

  • feature_set – Which feature set’s rows to rebuild.

  • extra_params – Further fixed model parameters that were in the search grid (none for the standard grid; used by the tests).

  • atol – Largest allowed difference between refitted and saved RMSE.

Returns:

A CVResult (model "mlp (tuned)") with per-fold scores and OOF predictions.

Raises:

ValueError – If no rows match feature_set, or a refitted fold’s RMSE differs from the saved one (the saved results then came from different code or data).

Predicted-vs-measured and RMSE-breakdown comparisons reuse functions.plot_results directly. save_png_pdf() writes every figure as PNG (for the HTML docs) and PDF (vector, for the report). The visual style matches functions.plot_results.

functions.plot_tuning.plot_inner_grid_heatmap(results: list[TuningResult]) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Heatmap of mean inner-CV RMSE over the grid, one panel per feature set.

Each cell is the inner-CV RMSE of one setting, averaged over every outer fold and seed. The outlined cell has the lowest average. Rows are network sizes (smallest at the top) and columns are alpha values, so a best cell on the border suggests the grid should be extended.

results – Outputs of functions.tuning.nested_cv().

functions.plot_tuning.plot_loss_curves(result: TuningResult, keys: list[tuple[int, int]]) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Training loss and early-stopping score per epoch for chosen models.

Top row: training loss (half the mean squared error on the standardised target, plus the L2 penalty). Bottom row: R² on the random 10% of rows that MLPRegressor holds back for early stopping. The dashed line marks the epoch with the highest validation score. Training stops once the score has failed to beat its best by more than tol for 20 epochs in a row; because tiny gains below tol do not count, the stop can come fewer than 20 epochs after the highest point. The final model keeps the weights from the best-scoring epoch.

Parameters:

  • result – Output of functions.tuning.nested_cv().

  • keys – (seed, fold) pairs to show (one column each).

Returns:

The figure (not shown or saved).

Entry point that tunes the MLP by nested CV and compares it with linear.

For each feature set, functions.tuning.nested_cv() tunes and scores the MLP on the outer folds, the linear baseline is cross-validated on the same seeds and folds, and the two are compared fold by fold. The test hold-out is never used:

python src/run_tuning.py                         # all seeds, sets A and B
python src/run_tuning.py --seeds 42 --feature-sets A   # quick timing check

Writes to results/:

  • tuning_outer_scores.csv: one row per (feature set, seed, outer fold): chosen setting, inner-CV best RMSE, outer RMSE/MAE/R², epochs run, max-iter hits and timings.

  • tuning_inner_grid.csv: mean and std inner-CV RMSE of all 35 settings for every (feature set, seed, outer fold).

  • tuning_selected_params.csv: how often each setting was chosen.

  • tuning_paired_vs_linear.csv: per-fold RMSE of MLP and linear and their difference (MLP minus linear).

  • tuning_summary.csv: headline numbers per feature set (see summary_row()).

  • tuning_oof_predictions.csv: every outer-fold (out-of-fold) prediction, one row per (feature set, seed, measurement), so per-setup analyses never need to refit (see functions.tuning.tuned_result_from_saved()).

  • tuning_warnings.txt: edge-of-grid and convergence warnings, if any.

Rounded tables and the figures (PNG + PDF) go to doc/generated/ for the HTML results page.

Error analysis¶

Where the models fail: spectral peaks and the error around them.

Analyses of the out-of-fold predictions, all on the cross-validation setups only (the test hold-out is never looked at):

  • spectral_peaks() finds the most prominent peak of each measured spectrum and the frequency at which a model’s predicted spectrum peaks.

  • peak_error_share() shows how much of each setup’s error comes from the frequencies around its measured peak.

  • tonal_table() gives each setup’s peak prominence.

Example

>>> from functions.error_analysis import spectral_peaks, peak_error_share
>>> peaks = spectral_peaks(data, mlp_result)       
>>> peak_error_share(mlp_result, data, peaks)
functions.error_analysis.PEAK_PROMINENCE_DB = 5.0¶

A peak must stand this many dB above the lower of its two neighbouring troughs (its “prominence”) to count. Below about 5 dB a peak is hard to tell from measurement scatter; the scaling conclusions were checked to be the same at 3 and 8 dB.

functions.error_analysis.TONAL_PROMINENCE_DB = 15.0¶

Peaks at least this prominent are treated as strongly tonal in peak_error_summary() (narrow spikes well above the broadband level).

functions.error_analysis.PEAK_WINDOW_STEPS = 1¶

Frequencies within this many 1/3-octave steps of the measured peak count as “at the peak” in peak_error_share().

functions.error_analysis.spectral_peaks(data: pandas.DataFrame, result: CVResult | None = None, prominence_db: float = 5.0) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Find each setup’s most prominent measured peak (and predicted peak).

Peaks are found with scipy.signal.find_peaks(), which only accepts interior points, so a spectrum that simply rises or falls to its end has no peak. Frequencies are 1/3-octave centres, so a peak frequency is only known to within one 1/3-octave step (about ±12%).

Parameters:

  • data – Dataset with physics features.

  • result – Optional model result; adds the frequency at which the model’s seed-averaged predicted spectrum is highest.

  • prominence_db – Minimum prominence for a measured peak.

Returns:

One row per cross-validation setup with the setup columns, has_peak, peak_hz, prominence_db, peak_index (position of the peak in the setup’s sorted frequencies), st_peak (peak_hz * disp_thickness_m / velocity_mps) and, with result, pred_peak_hz and pred_peak_steps_off (1/3-octave steps from the measured peak).

functions.error_analysis.peak_error_share(result: CVResult, data: pandas.DataFrame, peaks: pandas.DataFrame, window: int = 1) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

How much of each peaked setup’s squared error sits around its peak.

For each setup with a measured peak, the frequencies within window 1/3-octave steps of the peak form the “peak window”. If errors were spread evenly along the spectrum, the window’s share of the squared error would equal its share of the frequencies.

Parameters:

  • result – Model result.

  • data – The dataset the result was computed on.

  • peaks – Output of spectral_peaks().

  • window – Half-width of the peak window in 1/3-octave steps.

Returns:

setup_id, rmse (from the seed-averaged prediction), error_share (fraction of squared error in the window) and frequency_share (fraction of the setup’s frequencies in the window).

Return type:

One row per peaked setup

functions.error_analysis.peak_error_summary(shares: pandas.DataFrame, peaks: pandas.DataFrame, tonal_db: float = 15.0) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Median peak-window error share for all peaked and strongly tonal setups.

Parameters:

  • shares – peak_error_share() output for one model.

  • peaks – spectral_peaks() output.

  • tonal_db – Prominence threshold for “strongly tonal”.

Returns:

Two rows (all peaks, strongly tonal) with group, n, median_error_share and median_frequency_share.

functions.error_analysis.tonal_table(data: pandas.DataFrame, include_holdout: bool = False) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Peak prominence and chord Reynolds number of every setup’s spectrum.

The prominence of a peak is how far it stands above its surroundings: its height above the higher of the lowest points on either side before a taller peak (scipy.signal.find_peaks()). For each setup the most prominent interior peak is used, with no minimum, so every setup appears. A spectrum with no interior peak (it only rises or only falls) gets 0 dB.

Parameters:

  • data – Dataset with physics features (for the Reynolds number).

  • include_holdout – Include the test hold-out setups. Leave False for any analysis of model results; True is only for describing the whole dataset (exploration).

Returns:

setup_id, chord, velocity, angle, angle_band, reynolds, log10_reynolds, prominence_db and peak_hz (NaN when there is no interior peak).

Return type:

One row per setup

Figures for the error analysis (functions.error_analysis).

  • plot_tonal_by_angle() and plot_tonal_by_error(): peak prominence against chord Reynolds number for every setup.

The style matches functions.plot_results; save with functions.plot_tuning.save_png_pdf().

Entry point that finds the setups the models predict worst.

Each wind-tunnel setup (one chord, velocity and angle) gives one noise spectrum. This script computes the out-of-fold RMSE of every setup for the linear baseline and the tuned MLP, ranks setups by the MLP’s RMSE and plots the worst spectra:

python src/run_error_analysis.py                     # sets A and B, 10 worst
python src/run_error_analysis.py --feature-sets B --n-worst 5

The tuned MLP’s out-of-fold predictions are read from results/tuning_oof_predictions.csv, which src/run_tuning.py writes. If that file is missing (results from before it was added), they are rebuilt by refitting each fold’s chosen setting (functions.tuning.refit_outer_predictions(), about 30 s per feature set) and the file is written, so later runs can load it directly. Either way every fold is checked against tuning_outer_scores.csv. The test hold-out is never used.

It then runs three further analyses (functions.error_analysis):

  • an error map placing every setup on the test matrix, coloured by RMSE;

  • the share of each setup’s error that sits around its measured peak;

  • peak prominence against Reynolds number, coloured by the MLP’s setup RMSE.

Writes, for each feature set <fs>:

  • results/setup_rmse_<fs>.csv: every setup with both models’ RMSE and bias.

  • results/worst_setups_<fs>.csv: the worst setups by MLP RMSE.

  • doc/generated/worst_setups_<fs>.csv: a rounded copy for the docs.

  • doc/generated/worst_setups_spectra_<fs>.png and .pdf: their spectra.

  • results/spectral_peaks_<fs>.csv: measured and predicted peak per setup.

  • results/peak_error_share_<fs>.csv: per-setup share of error at the peak.

  • doc/generated/peak_error_share_<fs>.csv: rounded table for the docs.

  • doc/generated/error_map_<fs> and tonal_peaks_mlp_error_<fs> (.png and .pdf): the figures.

  • results/tonal_peaks_<fs>.csv: peak prominence, Reynolds number and MLP setup RMSE for every CV setup.

Robustness, physics check and acceptance criteria¶

Acceptance criteria for the final model, fixed BEFORE the hold-out evaluation.

Why fix them in advance? If the pass marks were chosen after seeing the hold-out score, it would always be possible to pick ones the model passes. Writing them down first, and committing this file on its own, makes the final check honest: the git history (commit 82c1b0d) shows the thresholds existed before the hold-out was used, and before the physics check had been written or run.

All criteria concern the final MLP (functions.models.FINAL_MLP) on functions.models.FINAL_FEATURE_SET, against the linear baseline on the same features. Every criterion is a blind test: its outcome was unknown when its threshold was set.

  • C1 Beats the baseline. The MLP has a lower RMSE than linear on the hold-out.

  • C2 Generalises. Hold-out RMSE ≤ nested-CV mean RMSE + C2_N_SD × the fold-to-fold SD (results/tuning_summary.csv). A hold-out score far worse than the spread seen across CV folds would mean the CV results were optimistic.

  • C3 Useful accuracy. Hold-out MLP RMSE ≤ C3_MAX_RMSE_DB dB. 3 dB is about a factor of two in acoustic power, a change a listener notices but which is small compared with the roughly 40 dB range of SPL in the data.

  • P1 Physics. The MLP predicts that faster flow is louder in at least P1_MIN_PAIR_FRACTION of speed pairs (same chord and angle), evaluated by src/run_physics_check.py on out-of-fold predictions.

Removed criterion (C1a). The original file also had “C1a: the MLP beats linear in at least 13 of the 15 nested-CV outer folds”. It was removed after the hold-out evaluation because it was not blind: the nested-CV results (MLP better in 15 of 15 folds) were already known when its threshold was written, so it could not have failed and was not an honest test. The fold comparison is still reported as supporting evidence on the results page, just not as an acceptance criterion. Removing it only takes away a criterion the model passed, so it does not make the final verdict more favourable. The original version is preserved in the git history.

Example

>>> from functions.acceptance import acceptance_table
>>> acceptance_table(tuning_summary, physics_pair_fraction=0.97)
functions.acceptance.C2_N_SD = 2.0¶

allowed hold-out RMSE = CV mean + this many fold-to-fold SDs.

Type:

C2

functions.acceptance.C3_MAX_RMSE_DB = 3.0¶

largest acceptable hold-out MLP RMSE (dB).

Type:

C3

functions.acceptance.P1_MIN_PAIR_FRACTION = 0.9¶

smallest acceptable fraction of speed pairs in the correct order.

Type:

P1

functions.acceptance.PASS = 'PASS'¶

Result labels.

functions.acceptance.FAIL = 'FAIL'¶

Result labels.

Evaluate every criterion that can be evaluated with the results given.

Robustness shift tests: do the models work on conditions they never saw?

Cross-validation holds out setups, but every held-out setup still has neighbours in training with the same chord and the same velocity. A shift test is harder: it holds out every setup with one chord (or one velocity), so the model must predict a value of that input it was never trained on.

  • Leave-one-chord-out: for each of the 6 chords, train on the other 5, test on the held-out chord.

  • Leave-one-velocity-out: for each of the 4 velocities, train on the other 3, test on the held-out one.

A held-out value between the training values is interpolation; the smallest or largest value is extrapolation, outside the training range, which is usually much harder.

Models: the final MLP (functions.models.FINAL_MLP) and the linear baseline, both on functions.models.FINAL_FEATURE_SET, built with functions.models.build_model() so all scaling stays inside the pipeline. Nothing is re-tuned. The MLP is repeated with random_state 0, 1 and 2 (MLP_SEEDS) to show the result is not down to one lucky weight initialisation; linear is deterministic, so it runs once.

Only cross-validation rows are used: the test hold-out is dropped first.

Chord and angle are confounded. High angles of attack were only tested on the small chords, so leaving out the 0.0254 m chord also removes most of the high-angle setups. A chord shift result therefore partly reflects angle, too. An angle-extrapolation test was deliberately not run for the same reason: holding out the highest angles would mostly hold out the smallest chord.

Example

>>> from functions.shift_tests import run_shift_tests
>>> table = run_shift_tests(data)
functions.shift_tests.SHIFTS = {'chord_length_m': 'leave-one-chord-out', 'velocity_mps': 'leave-one-velocity-out'}¶

The two inputs that are held out one value at a time, and the test names.

This is the accuracy on held-out setups whose chord and velocity were seen in training, so it is the baseline the shift results are compared with. It is read, not recomputed.

Parameters:

  • feature_set – Feature set of the comparison.

Returns:

{"mlp": ..., "linear": ...} mean RMSE over the 15 outer folds (dB).

Physics check: at the same chord and angle, faster flow should be louder.

Physics: for a fixed airfoil (chord) and angle of attack, a higher free-stream velocity produces more turbulent boundary-layer trailing-edge noise, so the overall noise level should rise with speed. The measured spectra in the BPM report (Brooks, Pope & Marcolini, NASA RP-1218, 1989) show this. A model that has learned real physics, not just patterns in the training data, should predict the same ordering.

Method (group_levels(), speed_order_check()):

  1. Use the cross-validation rows only (the test hold-out is dropped first).

  2. Group setups by (chord, angle). Keep groups tested at 2 or more speeds.

  3. Within a group, keep only the frequency bands measured at every speed in that group, so like is compared with like (a band missing at one speed would otherwise shift that speed’s average).

  4. For each setup, average the SPL over those shared bands: measured, MLP and linear.

  5. A group is fully correct if the predicted averages rise with speed in the same order as the measured ones. Each pair of speeds is also checked separately (faster predicted louder than slower).

Groups where the measured average does not rise with speed are listed and left out of the score, because the expected ordering does not hold there.

Why the predictions are honest. The predictions are out-of-fold: every setup was predicted by a model that never saw it during training. The MLP’s come from results/tuning_oof_predictions.csv, made by the nested-CV MLPs, where each outer fold used its own tuned setting (the final setting was the most common choice). The linear model’s come from functions.evaluate.cross_validate() on the same folds. Both are averaged over the 3 CV seeds.

Example

>>> levels = group_levels(data, mlp_result, linear_result)   
>>> groups, summary = speed_order_check(levels)
functions.physics_checks.MIN_SPEEDS = 2¶

A group needs at least this many speeds to be checked.

functions.physics_checks.MODEL_COLUMNS = {'linear': 'linear_spl', 'mlp': 'mlp_spl'}¶

Models compared, and the column holding each one’s mean SPL.

functions.physics_checks.group_levels(data: pandas.DataFrame, mlp: CVResult, linear: CVResult) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Final hold-out evaluation¶

Building blocks for the single final hold-out evaluation (run_final.py).

The test hold-out (fold == TEST_FOLD) is used here for the first and only time. Three models are trained once on all cross-validation rows and then predict the hold-out rows once:

  • mlp_final (functions.models.FINAL_MLP): the selected model; the acceptance criteria apply to it.

  • mlp_runner_up (functions.models.RUNNER_UP_MLP): a cheaper alternative, reported for comparison only.

  • linear: the baseline.

All three use functions.models.FINAL_FEATURE_SET and are built by functions.models.build_model(), so no setting is retyped and all scaling is fitted on the training rows only.

Hold-out predictions are stored in the same out-of-fold table format as the cross-validation results (functions.evaluate.CVResult, with seed = TEST_SEED and fold = TEST_FOLD), so the existing breakdown and plotting functions work on them unchanged.

The single final evaluation on the test hold-out.

Run this once. The test hold-out (fold == TEST_FOLD, about 15% of the wind-tunnel setups, chosen with TEST_SEED = 41 and stratified on chord) was never used for training, tuning, model selection or any analysis before this script. Here three models are trained once on all cross-validation rows and predict the hold-out once:

  • the final MLP (FINAL_MLP): the selected model. The acceptance criteria apply to it.

  • the runner-up MLP (RUNNER_UP_MLP): a cheaper alternative, reported for comparison only.

  • linear least squares: the baseline.

The selected model does not change because of these results. Model selection was finished using nested cross-validation only. If the runner-up scores better on the hold-out, that is reported, but the final MLP stays the selected model: choosing a model because it did well on the hold-out would turn the hold-out into another round of model selection, and it would no longer be an honest estimate of performance on unseen data. For the same reason, nothing is re-tuned, no threshold changes, and there is no second run to “improve” the numbers. If a criterion fails, it is reported as FAIL.

To make the once-only rule visible, the script refuses to run if results/holdout_metrics.csv already exists, unless --force is given:

python src/run_final.py            # about 10 seconds
python src/run_final.py --force    # only to regenerate identical results

Because every model has a fixed random_state and the same training rows, a forced re-run reproduces the same numbers; it cannot change the outcome.

Writes to results/:

  • holdout_metrics.csv: RMSE, MAE, R², bias, timings and epochs per model.

  • holdout_breakdown.csv: RMSE by chord, velocity, angle and frequency band.

  • holdout_setups.csv: the hold-out setups (chord, velocity, angle, rows).

  • holdout_setup_rmse.csv: RMSE per hold-out setup and model, ranked.

  • holdout_paired.csv: per-setup differences, final MLP − linear and final MLP − runner-up.

  • holdout_predictions.csv: every hold-out row with each model’s prediction.

  • holdout_vs_cv.csv: each model’s CV estimate next to its hold-out RMSE.

  • acceptance.csv: every acceptance criterion, now PASS or FAIL.

  • holdout_run_info.txt: when and with what code and settings it was run.

  • final_models/*.joblib: the three trained models.

Rounded tables and PNG + PDF figures go to doc/generated/.

Performance profiling¶

Runtime, memory, profiler and FLOP analysis of model training and prediction.

profile_model() fits a model on all cross-validation rows (the test hold-out is dropped first, exactly as in functions.evaluate) and measures:

  • Time: fit and predict are each repeated N_TIMING_REPEATS times and timed with time.perf_counter(); the median and the minimum are reported. The median is the typical time; the minimum is the least disturbed by other programs running on the computer.

  • Peak memory: with tracemalloc, which sees Python and NumPy allocations. Memory allocated directly inside compiled BLAS/LAPACK code is not seen, so the figure is a lower bound. Memory is measured in its own fit because tracemalloc slows code down and would distort the timings.

  • Model size: the number of fitted weights, their size as 8-byte numbers, and the size of the fitted model when saved with pickle. For an MLP the pickled file is about 3x the weights alone, because scikit-learn also saves the Adam optimiser’s two running averages per weight, which are only needed to continue training.

  • Epochs: for an MLP, n_iter_, the number of passes over the data before early stopping ended training.

  • Profile: a cProfile run of one fit, listing where the time goes.

  • FLOPs: estimates from formulas, not measurements (linear_flop_estimate(), mlp_flop_estimate()). Dividing them by the measured time gives the achieved FLOP rate, which shows whether a fit is limited by arithmetic or by Python and library overhead.

machine_info() records the computer and library versions, including how many threads the maths libraries were allowed to use, so the timings can be reproduced.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.physics_features import add_physics_features
>>> from functions.profiling import profile_model
>>> data = add_physics_features(load_airfoil_data())
>>> profile_model(data, "linear", "B").summary()
functions.profiling.N_TIMING_REPEATS = 5¶

Number of timed fit/predict repeats; the median and minimum are reported.

functions.profiling.N_PROFILE_LINES = 15¶

Number of functions listed in the cProfile report.

functions.profiling.linear_flop_estimate(n: int, p: int) → dict[str, float][source]¶

Estimate floating-point operations for the linear pipeline.

Counts for an n x p training matrix:

  • Input scaler: mean and variance (~3np) plus transform (~2np).

  • Target scaler: the same for one column (~5n).

  • LinearRegression: centring (~2np), then a least-squares solve with LAPACK gelsd (SVD based). For n >> p this costs about 2np^2 + 11p^3 FLOPs (R-SVD least squares, Golub & Van Loan, Matrix Computations). The 2np^2 term dominates.

  • Predict: input transform (2np), matrix-vector product (2np) and inverse target transform (2n).

These are leading-order counts for comparison with measured times, not exact operation counts.

Parameters:

  • n – Number of rows.

  • p – Number of input features.

Returns:

A dict with fit_flops and predict_flops.

functions.profiling.mlp_weight_count(n_inputs: int, hidden_layer_sizes: tuple[int, ...]) → int[source]¶

Number of weights and biases in a fully connected MLP with one output.

Each layer has (inputs x outputs) weights plus one bias per output. For example 8 inputs and hidden layers (128, 128) give 8*128 + 128*128 + 128*1 weights and 128 + 128 + 1 biases.

Parameters:

  • n_inputs – Number of input features.

  • hidden_layer_sizes – Neurons in each hidden layer.

Returns:

Total number of trainable parameters.

functions.profiling.mlp_flop_estimate(n: int, n_weights: int, n_iter: int, validation_fraction: float = 0.1) → dict[str, float][source]¶

Estimate floating-point operations for training and using an MLP.

Rule of thumb: one forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per weight per row (a multiply and an add), and the backward pass (computing gradients) about 4, so training costs about 6 per weight per row per epoch.

With early stopping, MLPRegressor holds back ceil(validation_fraction * n) rows. Only the rest are trained on (6 FLOPs per weight), but the held-back rows are scored with a forward pass every epoch (2 FLOPs per weight):

fit     = (6 * n_train + 2 * n_val) * n_weights * n_iter
predict = 2 * n * n_weights

This ignores the scalers, activation functions and the optimiser update (all much smaller), so it is an estimate, not a measurement.

Parameters:

  • n – Rows passed to fit (and to predict).

  • n_weights – Weights plus biases (mlp_weight_count()).

  • n_iter – Epochs run (n_iter_ of the fitted model).

  • validation_fraction – Share of rows held back for early stopping.

Returns:

A dict with fit_flops and predict_flops.

functions.profiling.machine_info() → dict[str, str][source]¶

Describe the computer, software and thread settings used for timing.

Thread counts matter: NumPy’s maths library (BLAS) may spread a matrix product over several CPU cores, which changes timings. The values come from threadpoolctl (installed with scikit-learn) and the OMP_NUM_THREADS / OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS / MKL_NUM_THREADS environment variables (“unset” means the library chose for itself).

Returns:

cpu, logical_cpus, platform, python, numpy, scikit_learn, the three thread environment variables, and blas (library name and threads in use).

Return type:

A dict of text values

class functions.profiling.ProfileResult(model: str, feature_set: str, n_rows: int, n_features: int, n_weights: int | None, n_iter: int | None, fit_time_s: float, fit_time_min_s: float, predict_time_s: float, predict_time_min_s: float, input_bytes: int, peak_fit_bytes: int, model_bytes: int, fit_flops: float | None, predict_flops: float | None, profile_text: str)[source]¶

Output of profile_model().

Variables:

  • model (str) – Name of the profiled model.

  • feature_set (str) – Name of the feature set.

  • n_rows (int) – Training rows (all cross-validation rows, no test rows).

  • n_features (int) – Number of input features.

  • n_weights (int | None) – Fitted weights plus biases (None if unknown).

  • n_iter (int | None) – Epochs run before early stopping (None for non-MLPs).

  • fit_time_s (float) – Median fit time over the timing repeats.

  • fit_time_min_s (float) – Fastest fit time over the repeats.

  • predict_time_s (float) – Median time to predict all n_rows rows.

  • predict_time_min_s (float) – Fastest predict time over the repeats.

  • input_bytes (int) – Size of the training input matrix as float64.

  • peak_fit_bytes (int) – Peak memory traced by tracemalloc during one fit.

  • model_bytes (int) – Size of the fitted model when pickled.

  • fit_flops (float | None) – Estimated fit FLOPs, or None if no formula exists.

  • predict_flops (float | None) – Estimated predict FLOPs, or None.

  • profile_text (str) – The cProfile report of one fit, sorted by cumulative time.

Return the headline numbers as one flat row.

A dict of every attribute except profile_text, plus weight_bytes (weights stored as 8-byte floats; None if unknown), and fit_mflops_per_s and predict_mflops_per_s (achieved rate: estimated FLOPs / median measured time, in millions per second; None without a FLOP estimate).

functions.profiling.profile_model(data: pandas.DataFrame, model_name: str, feature_set: str, n_repeats: int = 5) → ProfileResult[source]¶

Measure time, peak memory, size and the call profile of one model.

The model is trained on all cross-validation rows for the first seed in CV_SEEDS (the test hold-out is the same for every seed and is dropped first). This is the largest training set used during model selection, so it gives an upper bound on per-fold costs.

Parameters:

  • data – Dataset with every column the feature set needs (see functions.evaluate.cross_validate()).

  • model_name – Key of functions.models.MODELS.

  • feature_set – Key of functions.feature_sets.FEATURE_SETS.

  • n_repeats – Number of timed fit and predict calls.

Returns:

A ProfileResult.

Raises:

KeyError – If the model or feature set name is unknown.

Entry point that profiles runtime, memory, size and FLOPs of the models.

By default it profiles the models compared in the report, all in one session on the same machine so the numbers are comparable:

  • linear on feature sets A and B (the baseline);

  • the final MLP (functions.models.FINAL_MLP) on functions.models.FINAL_FEATURE_SET;

  • the cheaper runner-up MLP (functions.models.RUNNER_UP_MLP) on the same feature set.

Every model is trained on all cross-validation rows, never the test hold-out (functions.profiling.profile_model()):

python src/run_profile.py                                   # the four above, ~1 min
python src/run_profile.py --models linear --feature-sets B  # a custom selection

Writes to results/:

  • profile_summary.csv: one row per model/feature set: median and minimum fit and predict times, peak memory, model size, weights, epochs, estimated FLOPs and achieved FLOP rate.

  • profile_comparison.csv: final MLP vs linear (B) and vs the runner-up, as ratios.

  • profile_machine.csv: CPU, operating system, library versions and thread settings used.

  • profile_<model>_<feature set>.txt: the cProfile report of one fit.

Rounded copies of the summary, comparison and machine tables are written to doc/generated/ for the HTML results page.

run_profile.PROFILE_PLAN = [('linear', 'A'), ('linear', 'B'), ('mlp_final', 'B'), ('mlp_runner_up', 'B')]¶

(model, feature set) pairs profiled by default.

Exploratory plots¶

Histogram of the target, scaled sound pressure level (SPL).

functions.plot_spl_distribution.plot_spl_distribution(df: pandas.DataFrame, bin_width_db: float = 1.0) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot the number of observations in each SPL bin.

Bin edges are whole multiples of bin_width_db so bars line up with round dB values. Dashed and dotted lines mark the mean and median, so any skew in the target is visible at a glance.

Parameters:

  • df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

  • bin_width_db – Width of each histogram bin in dB. Must be positive.

Returns:

The created matplotlib figure (not yet shown).

Raises:

ValueError – If bin_width_db is not positive.

Overview scatter plot of SPL against every input feature.

functions.plot_spl_vs_features.plot_spl_vs_features(df: pandas.DataFrame) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot SPL against every input feature on a 2x3 grid.

Frequency spans several decades, so its axis is log-scaled. The unused sixth panel is hidden.

Parameters:

df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

Returns:

The created matplotlib figure (not yet shown).

Scatter plots of SPL against each feature, split by chord length.

functions.plot_spl_by_chord_length.plot_spl_by_chord_length(df: pandas.DataFrame) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot SPL against each non-chord feature, one row per chord length.

Chord length takes only a handful of discrete values, so splitting by it reveals trends that are blurred in the pooled overview plot. The y-axis is shared so noise levels are comparable across rows.

df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

Returns:

Scatter plot of SPL against each physics-derived feature.

functions.plot_spl_vs_physics_features.plot_spl_vs_physics_features(df: pandas.DataFrame) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot SPL against log-frequency, Strouhal number and Reynolds number.

Strouhal and Reynolds numbers each span two to three decades, so their axes are log-scaled. Log-frequency is already logarithmic and is plotted on a linear axis.

functions.plot_spectra_grid.plot_spectra_grid(df: pandas.DataFrame) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot every setup’s measured spectrum, arranged by chord and velocity.

Rows are chord lengths, columns are free-stream velocities, and each line is one setup (one angle of attack), coloured by angle. Axes are shared so panels can be compared directly.

Entry point that displays the exploratory plots for the airfoil dataset.

The plotting functions live in their own modules (functions.plot_spl_distribution, functions.plot_spl_vs_features, functions.plot_spl_by_chord_length, functions.plot_spl_vs_physics_features and functions.plot_spectra_grid); this script loads the data, adds the physics features, saves the figures used by the HTML docs to doc/generated/ and then shows every figure:

python src/explore_plots.py
python src/explore_plots.py --no-show   # only write the PNGs
explore_plots.DOC_FIGURES_DIR = WindowsPath('C:/Users/vasbr/OneDrive/Desktop/uni mech eng/2026s2/mma3001 numerical methods and machine learning/mma3001project/nummethodproject/doc/generated')¶
